en: Vehicles travelling toward you from the opposite direction.
An urban road where stopping is restricted during posted times, except briefly for passengers.
The main shopping street in a town or city centre.
A UK disability parking badge that gives certain parking concessions.
A very lengthy type of road vehicle, such as a lorry, coach, or articulated truck.
A car with an extended rear area for carrying more luggage.
An official authorised to manage traffic on motorways and some major roads.
Road markings at a junction where you must let other traffic go first.
A road marked with red lines where stopping and parking are tightly controlled.
A road marked so that stopping on the main carriageway is tightly restricted.
A speed limit that applies only for a limited time, often near roadworks.
An area where parking is controlled by signs and marked bays at set times.
Two white lines along the centre of the road that restrict crossing and parking.
Parking spaces reserved for vehicles displaying a valid Blue Badge.
A trailer designed for living or camping, towed behind a vehicle.
A system that warns you about vehicles in areas you cannot see in the mirrors.
Excused from a legal requirement for approved medical reasons.
Technology that helps the driver with safety, control, or alerts.
A child seat or similar device that holds a child safely in the vehicle.
An approved place that can safely take hazardous items like car batteries.
Shaking felt through the steering wheel while driving.
Older petrol that contained lead; not used for normal road cars today.
Cuts or damage in the side wall of a tyre that can make it illegal or unsafe.
Small stones on the road surface that can make tyres slip more easily.
A UK restriction meaning you must not wait or park there at the times shown.

A restriction meaning goods must not be loaded or unloaded there at the times shown.
Partly hidden or hard to see, for example by dirt, trees, or another object.
Lines, symbols, or writing painted on the road surface to guide or control traffic.
Small rectangular signs placed under a main road sign that add details such as times or exceptions.
A light on the instrument panel that alerts you to a vehicle fault or important status.
People injured in an accident or emergency.
An accident, breakdown, or other unexpected event on the road.
A side-lying first-aid position that helps keep an unconscious breathing person’s airway clear.

Police, fire, and ambulance teams called to help at serious incidents.

A policy that can cover costs after an accident, damage, or claim.
The official number plate details that identify a vehicle.
A UK personal tax and benefits reference number, not a driving document.
Move to the side of the road and stop safely.
Stops working so the vehicle cannot continue normally.
Scattered pieces of wreckage, objects, or rubbish left after a crash.

The official card that shows you are allowed to drive certain vehicles.

The liquid in the engine cooling system that helps stop the engine overheating.
Stuck inside the wound (for example glass or metal); do not pull it out yourself.
A lot of blood loss from a wound that needs urgent pressure and help.
A set of basic medical supplies for treating minor injuries at the scene.
Satellite navigation: a GPS device or app that gives driving directions.

Skin that looks unusually red or warm, for example from heat or emotion.

Passing a slower vehicle ahead by moving into another lane or the other side of the road.
A junction where one road meets another and ends, forming a ‘T’ shape.
A junction where two roads cross each other.
A side road joining the main road on a curve, which can reduce visibility.
Portable signals used for a limited time, often at road works.

Construction or repairs on the road that may change lanes or reduce speed.

The road becoming less wide, so careful positioning is needed.
A sharp uphill climb where the road rises quickly.
Gears with more engine power and less speed, useful on hills.

The annual UK roadworthiness test required for most vehicles over a certain age.
